pages.artDirection: Soft pastel 3D educational storybook, cute rounded characters, bright natural daylight, 11-year-old student context, short concrete A1 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Voice Note Challenge”, page 1. Scene based on: In a bright public school classroom in Medellín on a Monday morning, Laura, 11, and Tomás, 11, sit together at a desk leaning toward a phone that plays an audio wave icon, both frowning in concentration while classmates listen around them. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Every Monday, Ms. Elena sends an English challenge.
It’s always a short voice note in the class chat.
The students usually listen to it in the classroom.
Then they do the task at home.
Today, Laura plays the voice note on her phone.
Her friend Tomás sits next to her.
Ms. Elena speaks very fast this time.
The speaker on the phone is small and quiet.
“Bring a ... to class on Friday,” the message says.
Laura doesn’t hear one important word.
She looks at Tomás. “Bring a what?” she asks.
Tomás shrugs. He isn’t sure either.
The classroom is noisy, and the bell is ringing.

pages.artDirection: Soft pastel 3D educational storybook, cute rounded characters, bright natural daylight, 11-year-old student context, short concrete A1 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Voice Note Challenge”, page 2. Scene based on: In the classroom, three students hold their phones and speak at the same time with different gestures: one makes a plate shape with her hands, one draws a plan in the air, one holds a small potted plant; Laura and Tomás look confused in the middle. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Laura’s classmates have different ideas.
“She says ‘bring a plate,’” Sara says.
“No, she says ‘bring a plan,’” Pedro says.
“I’m sure she says ‘bring a plant,’” Tomás says.
Everybody is sure, and everybody is different.
Laura doesn’t know who is right.
She looks at her phone again.
“A plate, a plan, or a plant?” she says.
“These words sound very similar.”
Laura sometimes guesses when she doesn’t know.
But today she wants to be sure.
“Let’s listen again,” Tomás suggests.
“But this time, let’s listen carefully.”

pages.artDirection: Soft pastel 3D educational storybook, cute rounded characters, bright natural daylight, 11-year-old student context, short concrete A1 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Voice Note Challenge”, page 3. Scene based on: Laura and Tomás sit at a desk with headphones shared between them, listening to a phone screen showing a slow-speed icon of a turtle and an audio wave, Laura writing letters on paper with a pencil. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Laura finds the speed button on the voice note.
She changes it to “slow,” with a turtle icon.
They listen with headphones this time.
Ms. Elena’s voice is clear now.
She says the words very slowly.
“Bring a small plant to class on Friday.”
“We are going to describe it in English.”
Laura and Tomás look at each other and smile.
“I was right!” Tomás says.
“Yes, but we checked,” Laura answers.
“Now we really understand the message.”
They write the sentence in their notebooks.

pages.artDirection: Soft pastel 3D educational storybook, cute rounded characters, bright natural daylight, 11-year-old student context, short concrete A1 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Voice Note Challenge”, page 4. Scene based on: On Friday in the classroom, students hold small potted plants on their desks, a cactus, a basil plant and a small flower, while one student holds an empty plate and laughs; Laura shows her plant proudly to Ms. Elena. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Laura sends a reply to the class chat.
“I listened slowly. It’s a plant! Not a plate!”
She sends the slow voice note too.
On Friday, almost everyone has a small plant.
Laura has a basil plant from her grandmother.
Tomás has a little cactus.
Sara has a red flower in a cup.
But one student, Pedro, has a plate.
Everybody laughs, even Pedro.
Ms. Elena smiles. “Good job checking the message!”
“When you don’t understand, listen again or ask.”
Pedro laughs. “Next time, I’m listening slowly too!”

vocabulary.definition: a short audio message on a phone (nota de voz)
to pay attention to sounds or words (escuchar)
quick, not slow (rápido)
the part of a phone that makes sound (altavoz)
a living thing that grows in soil (planta)
to know what something means (entender)
at a low speed (lentamente)
to answer a message (responder)
a difficult task that tests your skills (reto)
on some occasions, not always (a veces)

quiz.question: What does Ms. Elena really ask the students to bring?
options: A written plan
A small plant
A pair of headphones
A clean plate
quiz.answer: A small plant

quiz.question: What happens AFTER Laura changes the voice note to “slow”?
options: Ms. Elena sends a new voice note challenge on Monday.
Pedro brings a plate to class on Friday, and everyone laughs.
Laura and Tomás hear the message clearly with headphones.
Sara says that the teacher wants a plate.
quiz.answer: Laura and Tomás hear the message clearly with headphones.

quiz.question: Read: “She says the words very slowly.” “Slowly” means…
options: in a different language
with a loud voice
very fast and quick
at a low speed
quiz.answer: at a low speed

quiz.question: What is the story mainly about?
options: A girl checks a fast message instead of guessing.
A class learns how to cook with basil.
A boy loses his phone during an English class challenge.
A teacher gives plants to all her students.
quiz.answer: A girl checks a fast message instead of guessing.

quiz.question: Why do the students have different ideas about the message?
options: The class chat deletes the voice note before Friday.
The three words sound similar, and the voice note is fast.
Some students do not have phones to listen to it.
The teacher sends three different messages to three different students.
quiz.answer: The three words sound similar, and the voice note is fast.

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “What Are We Wearing Saturday?”, page 1. Scene based on: In a public school hallway in Medellín, Julián, 12, and Sara, 12, read a colorful school event poster showing only icons of a sun, a soccer ball, a theater mask and a gym, while Julián points at the sun icon happily. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Saturday, Julián’s school is having Family Day.
There are games in the morning.
There is a show in the afternoon.
The games are outdoor activities in the courtyard.
The show is an indoor activity in the gym.
Julián is going to play in the soccer game.
“I’m going to wear shorts and sandals,” he says.
His friend Sara is reading the event poster.
“Are you going to check the weather first?” she asks.
Julián laughs. “It’s always sunny in the morning!”
Sara isn’t so sure about that.

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “What Are We Wearing Saturday?”, page 2. Scene based on: Julián and Sara look at Sara's phone showing a weather forecast with only icons: a big sun in the morning, a cloud with raindrops after one o'clock, and a thermometer, while Julián scratches his head. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Sara opens the forecast on her phone.
“Sunny and hot in the morning,” she reads.
“Then rain after one o’clock.”
“So we are going to need two kinds of clothes.”
Julián frowns. “What am I going to wear, then?”
“If it’s hot, I’m going to wear shorts,” he says.
“If it rains, I’m going to be wet.”
Sara thinks about the show in the gym.
“Wait. There’s one more thing we don’t know.”
“What are the rules for the gym?”

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “What Are We Wearing Saturday?”, page 3. Scene based on: In the school office, a friendly school secretary in her forties shows Julián and Sara a simple printed sheet with only icons of sneakers with a check mark and sandals with a red X, while Sara takes notes. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: They go to the school office to ask.
The secretary looks at the event information.
“In the gym, everyone has to wear sneakers,” she says.
“No sandals. The floor is very slippery.”
“And the gym is cold with the air conditioner.”
Julián is surprised. “So sandals are a bad idea.”
“Yes, and shorts might be cold inside,” Sara says.
“What are we going to do?”
The secretary smiles. “Wear layers. It’s easy.”
“You can take clothes off or put them on.”

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “What Are We Wearing Saturday?”, page 4. Scene based on: In Julián's bedroom, Julián lays out clothes on his bed: a T-shirt, a light jacket, jeans, white sneakers, a cap, a small bottle of sunscreen and a folded raincoat, while Sara gives advice on a video call. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: That evening, Julián and Sara make a clothing plan.
“I’m going to wear a T-shirt and jeans,” Julián says.
“I’m going to bring a light jacket for the gym.”
“And I’m going to wear my sneakers all day.”
Sara adds more ideas.
“Wear a cap for the sun in the morning.”
“Put on sunscreen before the games.”
“Bring a raincoat in your backpack for the afternoon.”
Julián puts everything on his bed.
“If the weather changes, I’m going to be ready.”

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “What Are We Wearing Saturday?”, page 5. Scene based on: At the school Family Day, in the sunny morning courtyard, Julián in a cap and sneakers kicks a soccer ball, then in the afternoon he sits warm in a jacket in the gym watching a theater show while rain falls outside the big windows. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Saturday morning, the sun is very strong.
Julián plays soccer with his cap and sunscreen.
Some students without caps have red faces.
At one o’clock, dark clouds cover the sky.
Then it starts to rain hard.
Everyone runs into the gym for the show.
Julián puts on his jacket. The gym is cold.
A boy in sandals can’t enter the gym.
He has to go home and change his shoes.
Julián looks at Sara and smiles.
“Good plan,” he says. “The forecast was right.”

vocabulary.definition: the condition of the air: sun, rain, wind (clima)
a report about future weather (pronóstico)
to have clothes on your body (llevar puesto)
outside a building (al aire libre)
inside a building (bajo techo)
a short coat for cool days (chaqueta)
sports shoes (tenis)
a soft hat with a front part (gorra)
cream that protects your skin from the sun (bloqueador solar)
clothes you wear one on top of another (capas)

quiz.question: What does the school secretary say about the gym?
options: The show in the gym is cancelled because of rain.
The gym is very hot in the afternoon.
Everyone has to wear sneakers because the floor is slippery.
Students can wear sandals in the gym if they are very careful.
quiz.answer: Everyone has to wear sneakers because the floor is slippery.

quiz.question: Why does Julián decide to wear layers?
options: He wants to look different from his friends.
His mother tells him to wear all his warm clothes on Saturday.
The school has a strict rule about wearing jackets at every event.
The morning will be hot, but the gym and afternoon will be cold.
quiz.answer: The morning will be hot, but the gym and afternoon will be cold.

quiz.question: What is the main idea of the story?
options: Checking the weather and the rules helps you plan the right clothes.
It always rains in Medellín after one o’clock in the afternoon.
Family Day is the best and most popular event of the school year.
Students should never wear sandals at school, even on hot days.
quiz.answer: Checking the weather and the rules helps you plan the right clothes.

quiz.question: Why can’t the boy in sandals enter the gym?
options: He forgot his ticket for the theater show at home.
The gym rules say everyone must wear sneakers.
He is too wet from the rain to enter.
He arrived late after the show started.
quiz.answer: The gym rules say everyone must wear sneakers.

quiz.question: Read: “The show is an indoor activity in the gym.” “Indoor” means…
options: outside a building
only for families
inside a building
very cold and windy
quiz.answer: inside a building

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “A Gift With No Name”, page 1. Scene based on: In a public school classroom in Medellín on Thursday afternoon, a beautifully wrapped gift box with a red ribbon and no card sits on the teacher's desk, while Diego, 13, points at it with curiosity and Sara, 13, holds paper decorations. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: The class is planning a celebration for Friday.
It’s Ms. Marta’s birthday, and she is their favorite teacher.
They’re having a small party at ten in the classroom.
On Thursday afternoon, Diego and Sara stay after class.
They’re making paper flowers to decorate the room.
Suddenly, Diego sees something on the teacher’s desk.
It’s a gift with blue paper and a red ribbon.
“Who put that there?” Diego asks.
Someone took time to wrap it very carefully.
Sara looks at the box carefully.
There’s no card and no name on it.
“That’s strange,” she says.

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “A Gift With No Name”, page 2. Scene based on: The next morning, a group of students crowds around the teacher's desk pointing at the wrapped gift and talking at the same time with excited gestures, while Diego looks uncertain and Sara raises her hand to calm everyone. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Friday morning, everybody is talking about the box.
“It’s from Pedro! He’s always generous,” one girl says.
“No, it’s for a student,” a boy says.
“Maybe it’s from Ms. Marta’s boyfriend!” another laughs.
Everybody wants to guess.
Some students want to open it.
“Let’s look inside! Then we’ll know,” a boy says.
Diego is curious too.
But Sara steps in front of the desk.
“We aren’t opening something that isn’t ours,” she says.
“Let’s find facts. Who was in the room yesterday?”

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “A Gift With No Name”, page 3. Scene based on: In the school office, a kind school secretary in her fifties with glasses talks to Diego and Sara, smiling and pointing at a visitor notebook shown only with lines, while a wall clock shows 9:15. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Diego and Sara go to the school office.
The secretary, Mrs. Luz, knows everything about the school.
“Did anyone visit Ms. Marta’s classroom yesterday?” Diego asks.
Mrs. Luz checks her visitor notebook.
“Yes. A young woman came at 3:30,” she says.
“She was Ms. Marta’s student ten years ago.”
“She brought a gift and asked me to keep it secret.”
“I’m putting the card on the gift at 9:30,” she adds.
“She wanted it to be a surprise.”
Diego and Sara look at each other and laugh.

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “A Gift With No Name”, page 4. Scene based on: Back in the classroom, Diego and Sara explain the mystery to their classmates in a circle, Diego holding a small white card, and some students look embarrassed while others smile. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: They run back to the classroom.
Mrs. Luz is walking behind them with a small white card.
She puts the card on the gift.
“So it isn’t from Pedro,” a girl says, embarrassed.
“And it isn’t for a student,” a boy adds.
“It’s from a former student,” Diego explains.
“She was in Ms. Marta’s class ten years ago.”
The students are quiet for a moment.
“Wow. Ms. Marta is important to many people,” Sara says.
Now the class is excited again, but for a better reason.

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “A Gift With No Name”, page 5. Scene based on: In the decorated classroom with paper flowers and a small cake, Ms. Marta, a teacher in her forties, opens the wrapped gift and finds an old class photo in a frame, touched and smiling, while the students clap. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: At ten o’clock, Ms. Marta enters the classroom.
“Surprise! Happy birthday!” the students shout.
The room has paper flowers and a small cake.
Then Ms. Marta sees the gift with the card.
She reads the card, and her eyes fill with tears.
She opens the gift carefully.
It’s an old class photo in a beautiful frame.
“This was my first class as a teacher,” she says.
“This student is a doctor now.”
Everybody claps for Ms. Marta.

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “A Gift With No Name”, page 6. Scene based on: After the party, Diego and Sara clean up the classroom together, Diego carefully removing paper flowers from the wall while Sara holds a garbage bag, both smiling and talking. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: After the party, Diego and Sara are cleaning the room.
“We almost opened that gift,” Diego says.
“Yes. And we almost blamed Pedro,” Sara answers.
“Guessing was fun, but it wasn’t fair.”
“The facts were much more interesting,” Diego says.
Sara nods. “And we know a new story now.”
Diego takes the last paper flower from the wall.
“Next week we’re writing her a card too,” he says.
“From all of us, with our names on it.”
Sara laughs. “Yes. No more mysteries.”

vocabulary.definition: something you give to someone (regalo)
to cover something with paper (envolver)
a small folded paper with a message (tarjeta)
a special event to enjoy something good (celebración)
the day each year when you were born (cumpleaños)
to give an answer without being sure (adivinar)
something you do not expect (sorpresa)
a person who works in an office (secretaria)
from before, not now (antiguo, exalumno)
to make a place look beautiful (decorar)

quiz.question: Who left the gift on the teacher’s desk?
options: Ms. Marta’s boyfriend, who lives in another city
Pedro, a generous student in the class
Mrs. Luz, the school secretary
A former student of Ms. Marta from ten years ago
quiz.answer: A former student of Ms. Marta from ten years ago

quiz.question: Why does Sara stop the students from opening the box?
options: The gift is not theirs, and she wants to find facts first.
She wants to open the gift alone later, after the party.
She already knows what is inside the box.
The teacher told her to protect the box.
quiz.answer: The gift is not theirs, and she wants to find facts first.

quiz.question: Why does the author include the scene in the school office?
options: To show that the school secretary is angry about the party.
To show how asking the right person reveals the real facts.
To show that visitors cannot enter the school in the afternoon.
To explain how to decorate a classroom.
quiz.answer: To show how asking the right person reveals the real facts.

quiz.question: What is the main idea of the story?
options: School secretaries keep all the gifts for themselves.
Teachers always receive expensive gifts on their birthdays.
Looking for facts is fairer than guessing about a mystery.
Students should open gifts that have no card.
quiz.answer: Looking for facts is fairer than guessing about a mystery.

quiz.question: Read: “It’s from a former student.” “Former” means…
options: from a different school
very young and new
famous in the city
from before, not now
quiz.answer: from before, not now

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The First-Aid Decision”, page 1. Scene based on: In a school sports court in Medellín during volleyball practice, a girl named Camila falls to the floor holding her ankle while Mariana, 14, and Felipe, 14, run toward her and other players turn in surprise. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: It’s Wednesday afternoon, and the volleyball team is practicing.
Mariana and Felipe are on the court with the team.
Camila jumps high to block the ball.
When she lands, her foot turns to the side.
She falls on the floor and holds her ankle.
“Ow! My ankle!” she cries.
The coach is in the office for a minute.
Everyone runs to Camila.
It’s a small injury, maybe, but nobody knows for sure.
Mariana feels her heart beating fast.
Camila’s face is pale, and her eyes are wet.

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The First-Aid Decision”, page 2. Scene based on: Around the injured girl on the court, five teenagers argue with different gestures: one holds a hot water bottle, one tries to pull off her shoe, one says to stand up, one holds a phone ready to call; Mariana and Felipe look at each other. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Everybody has an opinion, and everybody is talking.
“Put hot water on it. Heat might help,” says Laura.
“Take off her shoe and move her foot,” says Juan.
“Stand up and walk. It might go away,” says Pedro.
“Call an ambulance right now!” says Sofía.
Camila looks scared and confused.
Mariana thinks all these ideas can’t be correct.
Some of them might even be dangerous.
Felipe raises his voice a little.
“Wait! Does anyone here know first aid?”
The group goes quiet.
Nobody wants to give a wrong answer now.

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The First-Aid Decision”, page 3. Scene based on: Mariana kneels next to the injured girl, speaking calmly and holding up four fingers, while Felipe holds a bag of ice from the school kitchen and the others listen quietly. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Mariana slowly raises her hand.
“I took a Red Cross course last year,” she says.
“I’m not a doctor, but I remember the basics.”
She kneels next to Camila and speaks calmly.
“This might be a sprain. You shouldn’t walk on it.”
“We shouldn’t move your foot or put heat on it.”
“Heat may make it worse in the first hours.”
Then she remembers four simple steps.
“Rest, ice, a bandage, and lift your foot.”
Felipe runs to the school kitchen for ice.

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The First-Aid Decision”, page 4. Scene based on: Camila sits on a bench with her injured ankle raised on a backpack, an ice pack wrapped in a towel on it, while Mariana wraps a light elastic bandage around it and Felipe holds the ice in place. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Felipe returns with a bag of ice.
Mariana wraps the ice in a towel.
“Never put ice directly on the skin,” she says.
She puts it on Camila’s ankle for fifteen minutes.
Then she wraps a light elastic bandage around it.
“Not too tight,” she says. “Tell me if it hurts.”
Felipe puts a backpack under Camila’s foot.
“We should elevate it above her heart,” Mariana explains.
“That may reduce the swelling.”
Camila’s breathing becomes calmer.
“Thank you,” she says quietly. “It hurts less now.”

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The First-Aid Decision”, page 5. Scene based on: The coach, a man in his forties in a tracksuit, arrives quickly and kneels by the injured girl, checking the bandage approvingly, while Mariana explains what happened and the school nurse comes through the door. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: The coach comes back and sees the group.
“What happened? Who did this bandage?” he asks.
Mariana explains every step she took.
The coach checks the ankle carefully.
“It’s swollen, but you did everything right,” he says.
“Now we have to call her parents.”
The school nurse arrives a few minutes later.
“It might be a sprain,” the nurse says.
“But it may also be a small fracture.”
“She needs an x-ray at the clinic to be sure.”

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The First-Aid Decision”, page 6. Scene based on: The next day at school, Camila walks slowly with crutches and a bandaged ankle into the classroom, smiling at Mariana and Felipe, while classmates make space for her. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: The next day, Camila arrives with crutches.
“It’s a sprain, not a fracture,” she says.
“The doctor said the ice helped a lot.”
“She said heat might make it worse.”
Laura, who suggested hot water, looks surprised.
“I really thought heat was good,” she says.
“Many people think that,” Mariana answers kindly.
Felipe has an idea for the team.
“Maybe we should all take a first-aid course.”
The coach agrees and finds a course for next month.
The whole team signs up the same day.

vocabulary.definition: basic help for an injured person before a doctor arrives (primeros auxilios)
damage to the body (lesión)
the joint between the foot and the leg (tobillo)
an injury when a joint twists too much (esguince)
bigger than normal because of an injury (hinchado)
frozen water, used to reduce swelling (hielo)
a strip of cloth to wrap an injury (venda)
to stop and relax your body (descansar)
to lift something to a higher position (elevar)
a picture of the inside of the body (radiografía)

quiz.question: What does Mariana say about putting heat on the injury?
options: Heat may make it worse in the first hours.
Heat should be used with ice at the same time.
Heat might help if it’s very hot water.
Heat is the best way to stop the pain.
quiz.answer: Heat may make it worse in the first hours.

quiz.question: Why does Felipe ask, “Does anyone here know first aid?”
options: He knows that Camila is not really injured and only wants attention.
He wants advice from someone with real knowledge, not only opinions.
He wants to practice his English with the volleyball team.
He wants the coach to come back faster from the office.
quiz.answer: He wants advice from someone with real knowledge, not only opinions.

quiz.question: How are Laura’s idea and Mariana’s advice different?
options: Laura suggests an x-ray, but Mariana suggests walking.
Laura suggests calling the parents, but Mariana says it’s not necessary.
Laura suggests heat, but Mariana knows ice is safer at first.
Laura wants to elevate the foot, but Mariana does not.
quiz.answer: Laura suggests heat, but Mariana knows ice is safer at first.

quiz.question: What is the main message of the text?
options: Students should treat serious injuries alone, without any adults.
Coaches should never leave the court during practice.
Volleyball is a very dangerous sport for teenagers.
In an emergency, calm, informed actions beat quick opinions.
quiz.answer: In an emergency, calm, informed actions beat quick opinions.

quiz.question: Read: “It’s swollen, but you did everything right.” “Swollen” means…
options: bigger than normal because of an injury
tied with a tight bandage
very cold because of the ice and the towel
completely broken into pieces
quiz.answer: bigger than normal because of an injury

10.label: 10° Grade / B1 Beginner
10.title: At Least We Had a Plan

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “At Least We Had a Plan”, page 1. Scene based on: In a public school gym in Medellín decorated for a science fair with tables, posters showing only icons of planets and test tubes, Daniel, 16, reads his phone in shock at night, while Sofía, 16, hangs a banner on a ladder. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Saturday, Daniel’s school is having a science fair.
Daniel is the main student organizer.
The biggest activity is a robotics demonstration.
University students are bringing four robots at eleven.
Three hundred visitors are coming, with parents and children.
On Friday night, Daniel and Sofía are decorating the gym.
At nine o’clock, Daniel’s phone rings.
It’s a message from the university team.
“Sorry, our van broke down. We can’t come tomorrow.”
Daniel reads it twice and sits down on the floor.
“The best part of the fair is gone,” he says.
His hands are shaking a little.

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “At Least We Had a Plan”, page 2. Scene based on: Daniel sits on the gym floor holding his head while three classmates around him talk at once, one suggesting to cancel the fair with crossed arms, another waving a phone; Sofía stands calmly holding an old notebook. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Daniel’s classmates react quickly.
“We should cancel the whole fair,” Pedro says.
“Nobody will come without the robots.”
“People will be very disappointed,” another student says.
“The principal will be angry with us,” a third adds.
Daniel feels terrible. He planned this for months.
Sofía is calm. She opens an old notebook.
“Wait. What do we know for sure?” she asks.
“The robots aren’t coming. That’s one fact.”
“But what else is still happening tomorrow?”
Daniel looks up. He hadn’t thought about that.

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “At Least We Had a Plan”, page 3. Scene based on: Sofía and Daniel sit at a table in the gym reviewing a printed schedule with only icons of microscopes, volcanoes, a quiz and a robot crossed out, Sofía pointing at a page of the notebook labelled only with a big letter B. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: They look at the schedule together.
Twenty student projects are still coming.
The volcano experiment is still happening at ten.
The microscope table is still open all day.
The science quiz is still starting at two.
“Only one activity is cancelled, not the whole fair,” Sofía says.
Then she shows Daniel the old notebook.
“Remember our first meeting? You laughed at my idea.”
“I wrote a backup plan in case the robots failed.”
Daniel reads it slowly. It says “Plan B.”

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “At Least We Had a Plan”, page 4. Scene based on: Daniel smiles as he reads the notebook's Plan B, which shows only simple drawings of students doing experiments in front of an audience; Sofía crosses her arms with a proud smile. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Plan B is simple but smart.
“If the robots don’t come, students will do live experiments.”
“Each group will show one experiment in the main area.”
“Fifteen minutes each, from eleven to one.”
Daniel laughs, a little embarrassed.
“I said nobody will need a Plan B,” he says.
“At least we had a plan,” Sofía answers.
They make a list of possible groups.
The chemistry club has a color-changing experiment.
The physics group has a homemade rocket.
The biology group has a plant that moves when touched.

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “At Least We Had a Plan”, page 5. Scene based on: Late Friday night, Daniel calls classmates on his phone while Sofía writes a new schedule on a big poster with colored markers using only icons and arrows, the empty gym behind them. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Now they have to confirm everything tonight.
Daniel calls the chemistry club leader first.
“Are you coming at eleven tomorrow?” he asks.
“Yes, we’re bringing our materials,” she says.
Then he calls the physics group.
“We’ll launch the rocket outside at 11:30,” they say.
Sofía makes a new poster with the new schedule.
They also post a short message for families.
“The robots aren’t coming, but the science is!”
At midnight, everything is ready.
Daniel is tired, but he isn’t worried anymore.

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “At Least We Had a Plan”, page 6. Scene based on: On Saturday at the science fair, a crowd of families and children watches students do a color-changing chemistry experiment in the main area, gasping and clapping, while Daniel and Sofía watch from the side. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Saturday morning, the gym is full.
At eleven, the chemistry club starts the first show.
A clear liquid suddenly turns bright purple.
The children shout, “Again! Again!”
At 11:30, the physics group launches their rocket.
It flies high above the school courtyard.
The audience claps and cheers.
A visitor asks Daniel a question.
“Will you do this every year?” she asks.
“I hope so,” Daniel says with a big smile.
One small boy wants to join the chemistry club.
He is only eight, but he is very excited.

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “At Least We Had a Plan”, page 7. Scene based on: After the fair, Daniel and Sofía sit on the edge of the stage in the empty gym, tired but happy, Daniel holding Sofía's notebook with Plan B and pointing at it, confetti on the floor. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: After the fair, the gym is empty and quiet.
Daniel and Sofía sit on the stage, tired.
“Nobody asked about the robots,” Daniel says, surprised.
“The children loved the live experiments.”
“Next year, I’ll make a backup plan for everything,” he says.
“Not because I’m sure something will fail.”
“But because something might fail.”
Sofía laughs. “Now you sound like a real organizer.”
The principal walks in and thanks them both.
“You didn’t cancel. You adapted,” she says.
Daniel puts the notebook in his backpack carefully.

vocabulary.definition: a public event where projects are shown (feria)
a show of how something works (demostración)
to decide that a planned event will not happen (cancelar)
something ready in case the first plan fails (respaldo)
to make sure something is true or will happen (confirmar)
a person who plans an event (organizador)
a scientific test to learn something (experimento)
a person who comes to a place for a short time (visitante)
a plan with times for activities (horario)
the people who watch an event (público)

quiz.question: Why can’t the university team bring the robots?
options: The principal cancelled their visit.
Their van broke down.
The robots stopped working on Friday.
They forgot the date of the fair.
quiz.answer: Their van broke down.

quiz.question: Why does Sofía ask, “What do we know for sure?”
options: She wants to cancel the fair immediately.
She wants to know if the university robots are very expensive.
She wants to separate the real problem from fearful predictions.
She thinks Daniel is lying about the message from the university.
quiz.answer: She wants to separate the real problem from fearful predictions.

quiz.question: Why does the author include Sofía’s old notebook?
options: To show that Sofía writes better than Daniel.
To explain how university robots work in school science fairs.
To describe the decorations in the gym.
To show that a backup plan prepared earlier can solve a crisis.
quiz.answer: To show that a backup plan prepared earlier can solve a crisis.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between the robots’ cancellation and the live experiments?
options: The cancellation makes the team use Plan B, the live experiments.
The live experiments cause the robots to break.
The robots and the live experiments happen at the same time in the gym.
The live experiments were planned before the fair had robots.
quiz.answer: The cancellation makes the team use Plan B, the live experiments.

quiz.question: Which statement best summarizes the text?
options: Science fairs should always include robots from a university.
A backup plan can save an event when an important part is cancelled.
Students should cancel events when the first problems appear.
University students are always better at science than school students.
quiz.answer: A backup plan can save an event when an important part is cancelled.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Who Made My Phone?”, page 1. Scene based on: In a small phone repair shop in downtown Medellín, Andrés, 17, watches a technician open his broken smartphone on a bench with tiny screwdrivers, revealing the battery and circuit board, while Camila, 17, leans in curiously. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Andrés’s phone stopped working on Monday.
On Tuesday, he takes it to a repair shop downtown.
His friend Camila goes with him.
The technician opens the phone on the counter.
Inside, many small parts are revealed.
There is a flat battery, a screen, and a green board.
Tiny cameras and speakers are connected to the board.
“Each component was made in a different place,” the technician says.
“This phone traveled the world before you bought it.”
Andrés and Camila look at each other.
They have an idea for their English project.
It is due in two weeks.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Who Made My Phone?”, page 2. Scene based on: Andrés and Camila sit at a school library table with a laptop showing a world map with only icons of a mine, a chip, a factory and a ship connected by arrows, both reading with serious interest. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: They choose a question: “Who made my phone?”
At first, Andrés thinks the answer is simple.
“It was made by a famous company,” he says.
Camila disagrees. “It was designed by that company.”
“But was it really built by them?”
They research the main parts of a phone.
They read news, reports, and company websites.
The answer is much more complicated.
It takes them three afternoons to understand it.
A phone is designed in one country.
But it is made in many countries.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Who Made My Phone?”, page 3. Scene based on: Close-up of the library table where Camila points at a laptop map showing icons of mines in different continents, a pickaxe and rocks, while Andrés writes the names of minerals with simple element-like symbols in his notebook. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: First, they learn about the minerals inside phones.
Many minerals are needed for one phone.
Lithium is used in the battery.
Companies mine lithium in Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia.
Cobalt is also used in many batteries.
A lot of cobalt is mined in Central Africa.
“Child labor has been reported in some mines,” Camila reads.
Andrés stops writing.
“So children may be working for my phone?”
“In some cases, yes. That’s why it matters,” Camila says.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Who Made My Phone?”, page 4. Scene based on: Andrés and Camila look at a laptop screen showing a large clean factory room with rows of workers in white suits and blue gloves assembling phones on long tables, with only simple icons, Andrés looking surprised. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Next, they learn about the chips.
Engineers design chips in several countries.
But many advanced chips are made in Taiwan.
They are produced in very clean factories.
Then all the parts are shipped to big factories.
Many phones are assembled in China, India, or Vietnam.
Thousands of workers assemble phones by hand every day.
Some work long hours for low salaries.
“One phone is touched by hundreds of people,” Andrés says.
“And most of them are invisible to us.”

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Who Made My Phone?”, page 5. Scene based on: A large container ship crosses the ocean at sunset, then a cargo plane lands at an airport, and finally a delivery truck arrives at a phone store in a Medellín mall, shown as three small connected scenes in one illustration. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: After assembly, the phones are packed in boxes.
They are shipped across the ocean in giant containers.
Some are sent by plane when they are urgent.
In Colombia, they are received at ports and airports.
Then they are driven to stores in every city.
“Companies ship products thousands of kilometers,” Camila says.
“And we buy them in five minutes.”
Andrés calculates the distance of his phone’s journey.
It might be more than forty thousand kilometers.
That’s longer than the circumference of the Earth.
Camila can’t believe it.
“My phone traveled more than I have,” she laughs.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Who Made My Phone?”, page 6. Scene based on: Back at the repair shop, the technician shows Andrés a new battery in his hand while Andrés's opened phone lies on the counter, Camila holding the old battery and looking at it thoughtfully. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Friday, they go back to the repair shop.
“Only the battery was damaged,” the technician says.
“It can be replaced. The phone can be saved.”
“You don’t have to buy a new phone.”
Andrés is relieved and surprised.
“So repairing is better than replacing?” he asks.
“Usually, yes. Fewer minerals have to be mined.”
“But many people buy a new phone every year.”
Camila holds the old battery in her hand.
It is small, but it contains many valuable materials.
“What happens to this now?” she asks.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Who Made My Phone?”, page 7. Scene based on: At a recycling collection point inside a Medellín shopping center, Camila drops an old battery into a special e-waste container with a recycling symbol, while Andrés reads a small poster showing only icons of batteries and a green arrow circle. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: “Old batteries mustn’t be thrown in normal trash,” he says.
“They can be dangerous for the environment.”
“They should be taken to a collection point.”
“Some materials can be used again if we recycle them.”
Camila finds a collection point in a shopping center.
That afternoon, she and Andrés take the old battery there.
They put it in a special container for electronic waste.
“It’s a small thing,” Andrés says.
“But it’s one step in the right direction.”
Camila agrees. “Now our project has an ending.”
They take a photo of the container for their presentation.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Who Made My Phone?”, page 8. Scene based on: In a classroom, Andrés and Camila present a poster showing a phone's journey as a world map with icons, while classmates hold up their own phones looking at them with new curiosity and the teacher nods. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Monday, they present their project.
Andrés holds up his repaired phone.
“This phone was designed in one country,” he says.
“Its minerals were mined in at least three continents.”
“Its chips were made in Asia.”
“It was assembled by workers we will never meet.”
“And it was repaired in Medellín last week.”
Camila asks the class a question.
“How long do you usually keep your phones?”
Most students say only two years.
Some say they change phones every year.
The class becomes quiet and thoughtful.
“Maybe the best phone is the one we keep longer.”

vocabulary.definition: one part of a machine or device (componente)
the part that stores energy in a device (batería)
a natural substance found in the ground (mineral)
to take minerals from the ground (extraer, minar)
a very small electronic part that processes data (chip)
to plan how something will look and work (diseñar)
to put the parts of something together (ensamblar)
to send products by sea, air, or land (enviar)
to fix something that is broken (reparar)
to use old materials to make new things (reciclar)

quiz.question: What part of Andrés’s phone was damaged?
options: The chips on the green board
The screen and the cameras
Only the battery
All the components inside
quiz.answer: Only the battery

quiz.question: How does Camila change Andrés’s first answer about who made the phone?
options: She says the phone was made only in Colombia.
She says nobody knows how phones are made.
She proves that the company built every part alone in one factory.
She explains that a company designed it, but many people built it.
quiz.answer: She explains that a company designed it, but many people built it.

quiz.question: Why does the author include information about cobalt mines?
options: To show that some phone materials involve serious human problems.
To describe the job of a phone repair technician.
To show that Africa produces and sells most of the world’s phones.
To explain how batteries are charged at night.
quiz.answer: To show that some phone materials involve serious human problems.

quiz.question: Read: “Thousands of workers assemble phones by hand every day.” “Assemble” means…
options: to send finished products to other countries
to put the parts of something together
to fix something that is broken
to take minerals from the ground
quiz.answer: to put the parts of something together

quiz.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the text?
options: Students should buy a new phone every year.
Old phone batteries can be thrown away with the normal trash.
A phone comes from a global process, and repairing it helps.
Phones should only be bought from famous companies.
quiz.answer: A phone comes from a global process, and repairing it helps.
